---
title: "5.7 Overview of Ordinal DVs"
---

- If you are considering using linear regression for ordinal outcomes, consider *y\** standardized coefficients from the ordinal model as an alternative
  - Unlike multinomial logit, only requires estimating *J* -- 2 more parameters than linear regression (for the thresholds **τ**). So, relatively efficient model
- Before using ordinal models, consider:
  a. Is there a clear *y\** latent metric underlying the observed categories of your dependent variable? If not, ordinal models may not be the best choice
     - If yes, and the latent *y\** is of substantive interest, the ordinal model can greatly simplify interpretation
  b. Whether your DV is ordinal as Stevens defined it:
     - Categories are ranked on a **single dimension**
  c. Consider whether the **relationship** between your predictor and outcome variable is likely ordered in nature
- If either (b) or (c) are violated, the ordinal model can lead to biased conclusions
  - Even if you think (c) is likely to hold, **always do a sensitivity analysis** using a nominal model before accepting the results of an ordinal model

## Extensions of the ordinal model

- Even if you don't use the ordinal model much in your work, it is the foundation for other useful models. E.g.,
  - Graded response item response theory (IRT) models are based on ordinal logit
  - The *y\** derivation of the ordinal model is used for the derivation of nonlinear factor analysis models for ordinal items
    - These are methods used to scale continuous latent variables from ordinal observed items
    - More appropriate than factor analysis (which assume interval level latent variables **and** interval level items)
- Both IRT and nonlinear factor analysis (actually the same underlying model) are very useful scaling techniques
  - Covered extensively in the Item Response Theory section of my [Latent Variable Modeling](/teaching/lvm.qmd) course
